title: What Happens When Grading Costs Almost Nothing?
author: Marc Watkins
summary: Marc Watkins tests a narrow classifier model called Jev against his own writing assignments and reports what happens to assessment when scoring becomes effectively free. Jev does not generate prose; it scores, routes and flags on probabilities, which is why it runs orders of magnitude cheaper than frontier chat models, and Watkins puts a number on it at roughly ten cents for 430 requests. His argument is that ultra-cheap probabilistic scoring lands hardest on exactly the tasks that have always been expensive, which in education means grading, formative feedback and the analysis of student data. The move the piece makes is to shift the worry away from hallucination and slop, which this class of model largely avoids, and toward what rubric-driven automation does to writing itself. Watkins notes he abandoned rubrics six years ago for labor-based grading because students wrote narrowly to criteria, and concedes he would reach for AI grading if he taught a hundred students a term. He closes on the deeper risk that students stop writing for a reader and start composing for an algorithm, and asks faculty to apply the language of cognitive surrender to their own offloading, not only to students'.
points: Jev's cost structure comes from predefined choices and parallel probabilities rather than next-token generation, which is what makes near-free scoring possible.
Watkins extends the implications past the classroom to any system that screens people with rubrics, naming loans, mortgages, insurance and job applications.
Because the model returns a score and targeted feedback rather than generated prose, the usual complaints about hallucination and flattery do not apply.
The dashboard use case worries him more than the feedback use case, since cheap classification makes semester-long or degree-long tracking and intervention trivial to build.
He points to UC Davis's PAIRR program as the nuanced path, where students and instructors both critique the AI's role in feedback rather than deferring to it.
quotes: Jev is a new narrow LLM model that doesn't generate text-it's designed to classify, route, score, and choose actions, all based on probabilities.
When you think about how many areas of society use rubrics or other metrics to score responses or screen people, ultra-cheap intelligence hits like a bomb.
Give Jev a rubric, and it will score open-ended student responses for less than a pack of chewing gum cost when I was a child. I'm not kidding. 430 requests cost me about ten cents.

Higher Edu must seriously consider the ramifications ultra-cheap machine intelligence is going to have on historically resource- and time-intensive tasks, like grading, feedback, research, and data analysis.
On a much deeper level, I worry that we're seeing a shift that stops asking students to write for an audience and instead craft a message designed for an algorithm to process.
When you write to please a machine, you enter into a feedback loop that may not benefit your learning.
I used rubrics in my writing courses for a decade before abandoning them six years ago in favor of a feedback-focused labor-based grading model.
